prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength concept to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, opening new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second

statement.case_for: Having read all eight opening ballots, I move B036 to the top of my own list, above the IceCube case I ranked first. It is the only shortlisted candidate that four members place in their top three and that six of eight rank at all, and for reasons I can weigh as an instrument builder: the magic-wavelength idea is a single clear conceptual step, it was realised and then pushed by Ye's group to 10^-18 stability and accuracy, and the result has been reproduced and cross-compared by several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE). Calibration and systematic-error control are the entire achievement here, and that is the patient work behind a result the community believes. The consequences are concrete and durable: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for variation of constants and dark matter, relativistic geodesy, and the pending redefinition of the second. The two-name allocation is also the cleanest on the shortlist, which matters for a chair looking for a prize the committee can defend.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology has been recognised repeatedly (Hall and Haensch in 2005 for the frequency comb, Wineland and Haroche in 2012 for single-quantum-system control, with ion clocks in the same family), so the committee must show that lattice clocks are a distinct step and not an increment on earlier prizes. Katori and Ye also stand on the shoulders of other clock groups (Hg, Yb, Al+ ion clocks), and the redefinition of the second has not happened yet. If those arguments prevail, the more fully open observational window of B012 is the better choice, and I would not resist it.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks at 10^-18 are a first-order measurement advance, reproduced in many laboratories, with the second-redefinition path making recognition timely, and the Katori-Ye pairing is natural.
responses.response: I agree on both the science and the pairing, and I have moved my first-place vote from B012 to this view. I would add that the independent reproduction you cite is the decisive point for me. I am less persuaded by your second choice, B007: it is a compound of cavity QED, ensemble memories and network proposals, and you yourself say it is maturing but unfinished, with no deployed network. That makes three names hard to defend as one decisive contribution.

responses.point: The clock is a precision-measurement achievement of the first rank whose uncertainty is set by the atom, not the trap, and a two-name configuration is clean and defensible.
responses.response: Your reading of the physics is persuasive and, as a detector person, I am glad to have it from the atomic-physics side. I would press one qualification that you touch on: the committee must articulate why this is not covered by the 2005 comb and 2012 prizes. My answer is that those prizes honoured the enabling tools and the control of single quantum systems, while the lattice clock is a new class of many-atom standard, with systematics tested between laboratories. I would welcome your view on whether that distinction holds in the text of a citation.

responses.point: IceCube's diffuse neutrino flux and the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane associations are a decades-long instrument-driven opening of a new window, with Halzen and Spiering as a prize built around the instrument.
responses.response: We agree on the importance and I ranked B012 first alongside you. My concern, which your own maturity note shares, is that the diffuse flux is confirmed at lower significance by other detectors, but the strongest source associations rest largely on IceCube alone, so the astrophysics is not yet settled. We should also not underrate the attribution problem you raise: DUMAND and Baikal pioneers and the thousands in the collaboration make two names harder to defend than Katori and Ye. I would keep B012 as my first alternative and consider it more compelling in a few years, but I do not think it should block B036 now.

responses.point: Circuit QED opened a controllable regime of quantum optics on a chip, became the architecture of superconducting qubit experiments, and is reproduced in dozens of laboratories.
responses.response: I respect the importance and the maturity of B044, and I defer to you on the circuit-QED history since it is outside my expertise. My reservation is timing and attribution. You and Stefan Kroll both note that Wallraff is missing from the three credited names, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits has just recognised the same platform, so another superconducting-circuit prize now looks premature next to a result with no such overlap.

responses.point: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect gave a new classification of electronic phases, with the Z2 invariant from Kane and Mele and the HgTe observation by Molenkamp, although the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang theorists are missing from the credit.
responses.response: I take the science as read and rely on you for condensed matter, but the missing BHZ credit that you, Bernhard Mehlig and Eva Olsson all flag is, to me, a real obstacle for a three-person Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize: the experiment was a response to their specific prediction. For me, that is a stronger objection to B054 than the 2016 overlap. I would be glad to hear whether you consider the allocation fixable by a citation that credits the theory and the experiment as one discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and from ion clocks, so that the citation does not overlap earlier awards.

Whether Katori and Ye alone fairly represent a field with many contributing groups, including Hall and Haensch's earlier recognition, and whether the pending redefinition of the second should be awaited.

For B012, how much independent confirmation of the source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) will come from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD, and whether Halzen and Spiering adequately represent the pioneers.
I cannot judge the condensed-matter and quantum-information candidates (B022, B054, B044, B046, B007, B003) at depth and rely on colleagues and expert reviewers.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B036. I work in astroparticle physics and detector development and belong to the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, so I am a field neighbour of IceCube (B012) and the Event Horizon Telescope (B055) candidates, with no specific membership or personal tie to either that I am aware of. I would flag that proximity if either became the leading proposal.
